title: Cast and wrought iron gas mains still in service
note: Miles left in US gas distribution systems. The pace has slowed as the easiest miles were replaced; at ~1,000–1,500 miles a year the rest takes ~11–16 years.

title: Where the cast iron is left
note: Cast and wrought iron gas mains by state, end of 2022. The Northeast and Michigan hold most of what remains.

title: Power assets: age against design life
note: Years. Old does not mean failing: maintained wood poles outlive their book life, which is why inspection is recurring work.

title: Years to clear the old stock at today's pace
note: Derived from the backlog and the current replacement rate. Water utilities renew only ~0.8% of mains a year, a pace that would take ~125 years, while mains that break do so at ~53 years on average, so that backlog grows.

title: Drinking water: the $625B twenty-year need
note: EPA's seventh needs survey, by category ($B over 20 years). Two-thirds is pipe in the ground.

title: Lead service lines left
note: Millions of lines. The 2025 count from utilities' actual inventories is less than half the 2023 model.

title: Water mains: age and condition
note: Miles of US and Canadian water main (Utah State University 2023 survey).

title: US electricity use is rising again
note: Billion kWh. Retail sales (EIA Monthly Energy Review) and total end-use consumption including direct use (EIA STEO, Oct 2026). Use was roughly flat from 2015 to 2021 as efficiency offset growth.

title: Data centers are the swing factor
note: TWh a year (LBNL for DOE, Dec 2024). The 2028 range is 6.7–12% of US electricity.

title: Investor-owned utility capital spending
note: $B a year (EEI). Replacement and hardening are a large share, and utilities recover it through their rates.

title: New capacity additions: solar and batteries lead
note: GW of utility-scale capacity (EIA). New plants bring operations and maintenance work, much of it kept by OEMs or owners.

title: Forecasts of five-year peak-load growth keep rising
note: GW of added US peak demand forecast over five years, by report year (Grid Strategies). The 2024 figure is the headline; on FERC's basis it was 64–66 GW.

title: Who benefits from each demand driver
note: Darker means a stronger benefit. Most demand growth funds new construction; the drivers that favor maintenance are replacement capex, gas safety work, lead lines and nuclear life extension.

title: How many utility-system construction firms are there?
note: US firms in NAICS 2371 (Economic Census via NUCA). The count includes new construction and telecom, so the pool doing utility maintenance is smaller.

title: Establishments by sub-industry
note: Business locations by NAICS code from secondary compilations of Census data; directional only (W). Water and sewer line work is the most fragmented.

title: The scaled players by revenue
note: $B, latest fiscal year. Fifteen to twenty companies operate at or near $1B, though fewer than ten in any one sub-segment.

title: Scaled consolidators already in each unit
note: Named public and sponsor-backed consolidators per sub-segment (examples, not a census).

title: Exits, recaps and failures
note: Disclosed or reported deal values ($M, log scale). Specialists sold for the most; diversified roll-ups failed.

title: How the precedent platforms turned out
note: Count of the platforms profiled in this report, by outcome.

title: Addressable outsourced maintenance market by unit
note: $B a year, low to high estimate. Hover for the basis: utility spend pools multiplied by the share contractors capture.

title: Margins do not rise with size
note: Adjusted EBITDA margin against revenue (FY2025, log scale). Margin follows service mix and owned specialty equipment, not scale.

title: Even maintenance-heavy margins swing with execution
note: Gross or segment margin, FY2024 against FY2025 (%).

title: EBITDA margin from $50M to $500M of revenue
note: Percentage points, estimate. Overhead leverage and purchasing roughly cancel the cost of a holding company and integration: about +0.3 points net.

title: What these businesses sell for
note: EV/EBITDA. Small private deals trade at 6–8x; scaled utility-services companies at 11–16x. Lower-middle-market figures cover all industries (W).

title: Field headcount that can move between units
note: Share of each unit's field workforce in occupations that can work in the other unit (estimate built on BLS occupation data). Gas and water are the only real pair.

title: Fleet value usable by the other unit
note: Share of fleet value (estimate). Trucks and excavators move; bucket trucks, CCTV and lining rigs, leak-survey and NDE gear do not.

title: What each unit's field workforce does
note: Share of field headcount by occupation group (%, estimate on BLS anchors). Lineworkers, plant crafts and water specialists are not interchangeable.

title: What each synergy is worth
note: Basis points of revenue, low to high (estimate). Density inside a unit is worth the most; crews flexing across units is worth the least.

title: Candidates by unit
note: Counts from the candidate list below. Platform-grade means fit 4 or 5, recurring maintenance and not dependent on low bids; independent means confirmed as not owned by a sponsor or strategic.
